key_insight: Capability emergence in language models is governed by a no-partial-credit nucleation event: all required circuit parts must align in one stochastic attempt, and the rate depends on how many parts are still missing.
engineering_relevance: This provides a constitutive-rate-law view of training that can predict when capabilities appear, when they can be controlled or delayed, and how circuit-level interventions can recover learnability.
method: Fit a driven-nucleation rate equation with frozen constants across emergence, plasticity loss, and circuit control scenarios.
Tested shortcut-free circuit tasks and multi-scale Pythia ablations to compare missing-part effects versus partial-credit predictions.
Validated mechanism with a gated-attention toy model and intervention studies on query-key versus value slices.
evidence_signal: Across seven capabilities and three model scales, ablations left a median 17% of capability in 32/32 discriminating cells, and forward/backward predictions were strongly confirmed on held-out models and step-timed emergence tests.
watch_item: The rate-law appears scoped to conjunction circuits in transformers up to 1.4B parameters, so broader generalization and intervention transfer to other architectures remain unproven.
paper_title: The Kinetics of Training: A Driven-Nucleation Rate Law for Emergence, Plasticity Loss, and Circuit Control in Language Models
